title: Presumption of standing
short: A legally established parent should have presumptive standing to a real relationship with their child.
problem: Under ORC § 3109.042, an unmarried mother is the sole residential parent and legal custodian until a court orders otherwise. A father whose parentage is established must still petition before he has any enforceable parenting time.
proposal: Once parentage is established by acknowledgment or adjudication, presume standing to a meaningful relationship, and place the burden on the party seeking to limit it.

title: Rebuttable presumption of shared parenting
short: Equal or substantially equal parenting time, rebuttable on evidence of danger or unfitness, with written findings.
problem: Allocation under ORC § 3109.04 begins from open-ended discretion, so outcomes vary by county and judge and conflict is rewarded.
proposal: Start from equal or substantially equal time. Allow rebuttal on evidence of danger or unfitness, and require written findings when the presumption is overcome.
verify: Verify the current status of shared-parenting presumption legislation in the Ohio General Assembly before publishing copy that describes it as pending or absent.

title: Tie obligations to standing
short: Enforce parenting time as quickly and cheaply as child support is enforced.
problem: Support is enforced administratively and automatically. Parenting-time violations require a private motion, a lawyer, and months of waiting.
proposal: Create an administrative enforcement option for parenting time, presumptive make-up time, and fee-shifting for unjustified interference.

title: Outcome measurement mandate
short: Publish anonymized, longitudinal outcome data on contested custody orders.
problem: Courts track filings, time to disposition, and collections. They do not track how children fare five or ten years after a contested order.
proposal: Require the Supreme Court of Ohio or ODJFS to publish anonymized longitudinal outcome data broken out by type of order.

title: GAL and evaluator reform
short: Rate transparency, rotation, evidence-based reports, conflict disclosure, and a complaint process with teeth.
problem: Guardians ad litem and evaluators carry great weight, are often paid by the parties, and face limited outside correction.
proposal: Adopt fee caps and published rates, rotate appointments, require written reports that state their evidentiary basis, mandate conflict-of-interest disclosure, and create an effective complaint process.

title: Weaken the conflict gradient
short: Early mediation, default schedules, and limits on repetitive motions.
problem: The system's resources flow toward prolonged dispute. Families that settle quickly generate little for it.
proposal: Default to early mediation (with DV screening), adopt default parenting schedules, limit repetitive motions, and review fee structures that reward prolonged litigation.

title: Imputed income limits
short: Evidence thresholds, time limits, and mandatory review before imputing income.
problem: Support can be set on income a parent does not earn, based on the court's estimate of what they could earn.
proposal: Require specific evidence before imputing income, limit how long imputation lasts, and require periodic review.

title: Arrears and enforcement proportionality
short: Modification windows, forgiveness pathways, and limits on punitive suspensions after involuntary income loss.
problem: Arrears accumulate quickly after job loss, and license or passport suspension can make repayment harder.
proposal: Allow retroactive-modification windows, create forgiveness pathways, and cap punitive license and passport suspensions where non-payment follows involuntary income loss.

title: Evidence standards for allegations
short: Findings before restricting contact on unadjudicated allegations, expedited hearings, and consequences for knowingly false claims.
problem: Contact can be restricted for long periods on allegations that are never adjudicated.
proposal: Require findings before contact is restricted beyond an emergency period, guarantee expedited hearings on emergency restrictions, and impose consequences for knowingly false allegations.
protections: Ex parte and emergency civil protection orders for genuine danger remain fast and low-barrier. This proposal shortens the time to a hearing; it does not raise the bar for emergency protection.

title: Dissent is information
short: A protected process for procedural objections, and a rule that objecting is not evidence of 'high conflict.'
problem: A parent who challenges a recommendation or a process risks being labeled 'high conflict,' so protest becomes evidence against the protester.
proposal: Create a formal process for procedural objections that requires a written response, and bar treating process complaints as evidence of high conflict without independent findings.

title: Extended family standing
short: Recognize siblings and grandparents as stakeholders.
problem: Siblings and grandparents appear in custody decisions, if at all, only as factors in someone else's case. Grandparents who provided years of daily care can lose all contact overnight, and unless a qualifying case is open, or after a child moves out of state, they may have no forum in which to be heard.
proposal: Clarify and strengthen standing for siblings and grandparents to seek companionship and continued contact. Give relatives who served as substantial, regular caregivers for a defined period a forum to request continued contact, with a fit parent's decision still given special weight. Require guardians ad litem to interview adults who provide substantial care, and to state in their reports whether they did.
protections: A fit parent's decision keeps the special weight required by Troxel v. Granville. Where a parent limits a relative's contact because of abuse, threats, or danger, that decision stays protected, and emergency protection orders remain fast and low-barrier.
verify: Verify how Ohio courts apply Troxel and Harrold v. Collier to relative visitation, and how ORC Chapter 3127 treats grandparent visitation after an interstate move, before describing current law.

title: Data and public-records transparency
short: Make court-operations data public and comparable across all 88 counties.
problem: County-level data on custody outcomes, GAL appointments, and contempt filings is hard to obtain and harder to compare.
proposal: Publish standardized county-level court operations data and make it routinely available under the Public Records Act.

title: Supervision with an exit
short: Supervised parenting time with a review date, written step-down criteria, and costs that don't end contact when the money runs out.
problem: Supervised parenting time is often paid for by the supervised parent, has no end date, and has no stated criteria for stepping down. When the parent can't keep paying, contact stops, even though no court found that it should. Meanwhile the supervised parent is monitored by paid, reporting professionals, and the other parent's obligations under the same order are monitored by no one.
proposal: Require every supervised-time order to state its reason, its review date (no more than 90 days out), and the specific criteria for moving to less restrictive time. Require findings to continue supervision past review. Provide sliding-scale or court-funded supervision so that contact never ends only because a parent can't afford it. Track both parents' compliance with the order with equal rigor.
protections: Supervision stays available, and stays in place, wherever a court finds a real risk to the child. This proposal requires that the risk be stated and reviewed. It does not remove supervision where danger has been shown.
verify: Verify how Ohio counties currently fund supervised visitation centers, and whether any local rules already require review dates for supervised orders, before describing current practice.

title: Treatment is not testimony
short: Seeking mental-health or substance treatment, or not seeking it, is not evidence of unfitness without independent findings.
problem: In a contested case, a parent's therapy and treatment records can be ordered disclosed, reviewed by court appointees, and tied to progress toward parenting time. A parent who doesn't seek treatment can be described as in denial. Both choices can be counted against the parent, so the rational move is often to avoid care, which is the worst outcome for the parent and the child.
proposal: Require a specific showing of relevance to the child's safety before treatment records are disclosed, with in camera review and disclosure limited to what bears on that question. Bar adverse inferences from either seeking or declining treatment without independent evidence of risk. Require that appointees who receive records use them only for the stated purpose.
protections: Courts keep full authority to consider a parent's mental health and substance use where independent evidence shows they bear on a child's safety. This proposal limits fishing expeditions and penalty-by-inference. It does not hide real danger.
verify: Verify how Ohio courts currently treat physician and counselor privilege when mental health is raised in a custody case, including waiver doctrine, before describing current law.
